description: try/catch, throwing, and handling errors like a pro.

screens.body:
When Java hits a problem it can't ignore — dividing by zero, opening a missing file, parsing 'abc' as a number — it creates an exception object describing what went wrong and throws it.

If nothing catches it, the program crashes and prints a stack trace: the chain of method calls that led to the failure. Stack traces look scary but they're treasure maps — read them top-down.

Common names to recognize: NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, NumberFormatException, IOException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

code.snippet:
int age = Integer.parseInt("abc");
// throws NumberFormatException -> program crashes

screens.heading: Errors have names
screens.keyPoint: An exception is an object describing an error.

screens.body:
Wrap risky code in try. If it throws, Java jumps straight to the matching catch block instead of crashing — and your program keeps running afterward.

The catch names the exception type it handles: catch (NumberFormatException e). Only that type (or its children) gets caught here; anything else keeps flying.

Inside the catch, e holds the exception object. e.getMessage() often has the useful detail — print it or log it so future-you knows what happened.

options: Keeps running after the catch block
check.question: After an exception is caught, the program…

screens.heading: try/catch: the safety net
screens.keyPoint: try the risky code, catch the failure, keep going.

screens.body:
A finally block runs whether the try succeeded, threw, or even returned early. It's the cleanup crew: close the file, release the connection, unlock the resource.

This matters because exceptions can skip your normal cleanup lines. Code after the risky call never runs if the call throws — but finally always does.

You'll see try-finally constantly in file and database code. When in doubt about cleanup, finally is the answer.

options: Only when an exception is thrown
check.question: A finally block runs…

screens.heading: finally: always runs

screens.body:
You don't just catch exceptions — you can raise them. When a method receives bad input, throw new IllegalArgumentException("age can't be negative") stops the nonsense immediately with a clear message.

This is input validation with teeth: instead of letting a negative age quietly corrupt everything downstream, you fail fast and loudly at the source.

Pick the exception type that fits: IllegalArgumentException for bad arguments, IllegalStateException for 'not now' situations, or define your own by extending Exception.
screens.heading: Throw your own
screens.keyPoint: throw new … = fail fast with a clear message.

screens.body:
Some methods might throw, and Java makes them say so: public void read() throws IOException. That throws in the signature is a warning label for every caller.

Callers then have two choices: catch it in try/catch, or add throws IOException to their own signature and pass the warning up the chain.

This only applies to checked exceptions (next screen). It's Java's way of forcing you to think about failure — annoying, but it kills entire categories of 'oops I forgot' bugs.

check.question: `throws IOException` in a method signature means…

screens.heading: throws: the warning label
screens.keyPoint: throws = 'this method might throw — handle it.'

screens.body:
Java splits exceptions in two. Checked exceptions (like IOException) MUST be caught or declared with throws — the compiler enforces it. They're for recoverable, expected problems: missing files, network hiccups.

Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its children: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, ArithmeticException) don't need declaring. They're for programmer mistakes — bugs you should fix, not plan around.

Practical rule: catch what you can sensibly recover from; fix the rest. And never catch Exception 'just in case' — it hides bugs.
screens.heading: Checked vs unchecked
screens.keyPoint: Checked = must handle. Unchecked = usually a bug.

screens.body:
Habit one: catch the most specific type you can handle. catch (NumberFormatException e) beats catch (Exception e) — the broad catch swallows bugs you wanted to see.

Habit two: never leave a catch block empty. At minimum, log or print something. Silent catches turn small bugs into mysteries.

Habit three: one catch can handle several types with multi-catch: catch (IOException | SQLException e). Same handling, less repetition.
screens.heading: Catch habits that save you
screens.keyPoint: Specific catches, never empty, multi-catch when handy.

screens.body:
Oracle's exceptions trail covers the full hierarchy, checked vs unchecked, and best practices straight from the language designers.

Exceptions trail: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/essential/exceptions/
